entries.title: The Nvidia Shield TV Is 7 Years Old. It Just Got a $100 Price Hike
entries.summary: The price of anything with memory is skyrocketing thanks to AI. Aging streaming devices are no exception.
entries.content:
The era of generative AI has upended technology supply chains, and there is one ironclad rule in 2026: If it has memory or storage, it’s getting more expensive. Even devices with years-old tech inside are still apparently subject to that unwritten rule. Nvidia has just announced that the Shield TV Pro is getting $100 more expensive, effective immediately.

The most recent version of the Shield streaming box debuted in 2019, running Android TV with AI upscaling and hardware decoding for almost any type of media. While it ran an aging Tegra X1+ processor, that was (and still is) fast for a TV media streamer. The device launched at $199.99, with a non-Pro variant at $149.99. The non-Pro Shield has since been discontinued, but the Shield TV Pro lives on at the new $299.99 price.

Nvidia has confirmed that you can blame AI for the higher Shield TV pricing. “Starting October 2, SHIELD Pro will be priced at $299. The cost of components, including memory, has increased substantially across the industry,” a spokesperson told Ars.

When Ars Technica talked to Nvidia’s Andrew Bell earlier this year, he framed the Shield as a passion project, but it looks like passion projects still have to pay the bills at Nvidia. In that interview, Bell explained that Nvidia still actively manufactures the Shield and sells every unit it makes. Without a stockpile of pre-AI hardware to sell, new Shield TV units are subject to the same supply chain constraints as today’s smartphones and computers.

Nvidia isn’t a victim here, though. As a key player in AI hyper scaling, the company is more responsible than most for the sky-high cost of components. It has also become one of the most valuable firms in the world thanks to its market-leading AI accelerators and GPUs. As a consequence, we’re seeing new products launch at higher prices than their predecessors, and many end up getting more expensive during their lifetimes. Game consoles have been particularly affected, with Nintendo, Microsoft, and Sony all bumping the prices of their current-gen hardware. The PS5 Pro, for example, has gone from $699.99 at launch in 2024 to $899.99 today.

Stock of the Shield TV Pro has been slim for the last few months, probably because it became too expensive to manufacture new units with component prices rising so quickly. At $300, it will make sense for Nvidia to churn out more devices. However, this higher price will cause an already niche set-top box to be even less appealing to people who just want to stream Netflix.

Unless you need the Shield’s extensive codec support or Plex server capability, it makes more sense to get a cheaper streamer. The Shield is still out of stock on Nvidia’s store, but it’s available at the new price from Best Buy.

This story originally appeared on Ars Technica.

entries.title: Muse Creates Detailed Profiles of All Your Friends and Family
entries.summary: Millions have downloaded Meta’s AI agent Muse. But getting it to do your bidding comes with privacy costs.
entries.content:
Welcome to Kernel Panic!, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

Meta’s new personal assistant, Muse, has become a viral hit, with millions downloading the AI agent, connecting it to bank accounts, messages, or health data, and allowing it to complete tasks for them. But as Muse takes off among consumers, data from inside the app is providing insight into how it organizes and presents information to users.

In recent days, multiple researchers have extracted Muse’s internal files and dumped the agent’s operating instructions, providing a glimpse of how the system was built and behaves. Meta has maintained that it intended for these files to be accessible in the interest of transparency, and they do provide insight into how Muse responds to prompts and questions about, for example, highly politicized or sensitive topics.

Independent AI safety and security researcher Karan Joshi was able to extract an extensive array of Muse instructions and system prompts by using the regular chat interface to essentially ask Muse to copy and share its own software files. Joshi then shared his findings with WIRED.

One of Muse’s instructions appears to be the ability for it to create “a page for every person in the user’s life.” This hourly process involves compiling data on family, partners, friends, colleagues, “collaborators,” and people you “follow,” the instructions say.

The general idea is that Muse can use its “memory” (aka structured text files) to collect information about your relationships and the important people in your life. It can then make suggestions, like giving pointers on how to improve particular relationships or, say, where to take a coffee-loving friend for breakfast. Of course, it’s not unusual for AI chatbots to track social information in general—people have been asking ChatGPT for relationship advice for years now. But it’s interesting to see how Muse is set up given Meta’s history and vast access to social network data.

“What it seemed like to me—from all these prompts, system skills data, and things that they’re feeding into Muse—is that they want to understand your relationships that you have with real people,” says Joshi. “They’re trying to know you like a friend, which is honestly pretty creepy.”

Muse’s documentation says that a page may start “sparse” and then be filled out over time, potentially including sections like Facts, History, The relationship, In common, Open threads, and Strengthening. Meta’s instructions say Muse should only use the “evidence” it has available, and that invented details are worse than an empty page.

“Where they live, what they do, the threads that recur (the apartment move, the shared savings goal),” the instructions say. They add, too, that the model could record the “dates that matter,” such as birthdays or anniversaries. A person’s history could include backstory like “the trip in March, the argument that got resolved, the milestone last week.”

The instructions also focus on recording relationship details such as “how close they are, what it is built on, how they act with each other, and what it seems to need right now.” The Strengthening section suggests ways a relationship could be improved, including, “A reason to call, a date worth remembering, something they said to circle back on, a way to be there for them that matters.”

“We are giving AI systems much more information about us than we are getting information from them,” says Carissa Véliz, an associate professor at Oxford’s Institute for Ethics in AI. “It’s not only what we explicitly tell them, but what they can infer from us—correctly or incorrectly, both concerning for different reasons—and what they can piece together from other sources of data.”

Muse is architected so each individual user has their own dedicated virtual machine, which stores user data and context. This VM is inaccessible to other agents and users can wipe memories or disconnect external services at any time. Meta says that Muse is also designed to seek human confirmation before completing actions like sending an email or making a purchase, and that it has an audit log where users can see all of the agent’s activity and future plans.

“For any agent to be useful and actually help you achieve your goals, it needs to have context about you and those you interact with,” Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts told WIRED in a statement. “Muse gathers that based on public information and from what you’ve chosen to share, which is how it remembers the person who sent you an invoice is in fact the plumber who you previously hired to complete work in your bathroom or which flowers your spouse said they liked best.”

It’s become common for AI assistants to incorporate some sort of memory feature designed to allow greater personalization in responses and activity. Miranda Bogen, the director of the Center for Democracy and Technology’s AI Governance Lab, says Muse appears to have more emphasis on relationships and personal contacts than rivals’ systems. In general, these tools tend to offer some transparency and editing capabilities, and Muse does as well. If anything, though, Bogen notes that agents and assistants encourage people to proactively share more data with them versus focusing on culling data.

“These [AI assistant] tools are actively soliciting users to plug their whole lives in—their emails, calendars, financial institutions, everything in order to be helpful assistance,” Bogen says. “That’s dramatically more information than people might have otherwise given to some of these companies. The breadth of access to information that these tools have will lead to a ballooning of what they know about users.

Spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at [email protected]. And stay safe out there.

entries.title: How to Collect CDs
entries.summary: Fed up with paying to stream music you’ll never actually own? Give the little silver disc a spin. Here’s how to start a CD collection or get more out of one you already have.
entries.content:
When I started collecting physical media in 2009 at 13 years old, CDs still dominated the market. Big-box retail stores had music sections with rows and rows of sealed jewel cases, and it was normal to spend $25 on a deluxe album or a box set.

Less than a decade later, streaming had taken over. Vinyl records outsold CDs for the first time in 2022. The Compact Disc began to feel like an afterthought.

But now the CD is enjoying a surge in popularity thanks to cultural shifts like the rise in K-pop, the backlash against the streaming platforms’ policies, and Gen-Zers driving hand-me-down cars without Bluetooth connectivity. When I walked into a record store in July and found a deluxe CD for Madonna’s new album, Confessions II, on sale for $34, more expensive than some of the vinyl pressings, it finally felt like the format was officially back. (And yes, I bought it.)

According to 2026 data from the entertainment industry research firm Luminate, K-pop groups like BTS, Enhypen, and ATEEZ contributed to an overall 16 percent increase in CD sales so far this year, thanks to collectible editions that encouraged fans to buy multiple copies of the groups’ albums. This seems to be the major shift between the old way of buying music and the new normal: CDs are looked at more as merch—collectibles that support the artist—than as necessities to hear the songs. According to the same Luminate report, if K-pop were taken out of the data, disc sales would’ve still increased 6.7 percent.

Though the numbers show solid growth, CDs are nowhere near as hot as they used to be. The music industry sold 16.3 million discs in the first half of this year, a paltry number compared to the CD’s heyday around the turn of the millennium, when annual sales topped 900 million. Still, their collectible physicality has brought them back into fashion.

There really is no right or wrong way to collect CDs. If you keep a CD in its packaging, it will be protected for years to come. But here are some tips if you want to elevate your collecting experience and get more out of your collection, whether you’re new to the format or rescuing an old box of discs from the garage.

Get a CD Player

It might seem that owning a CD player is the obvious first step to collecting CDs. But according to Luminate’s report, only half of millennials and Gen-Zers that collect CDs have a player. Luckily, finding a good CD player is easier and more budget-friendly than buying a record player.

You might even have a CD player without knowing it; a Blu-ray player hooked up to a nice sound bar is a convenient set up to play CDs, since most Blu-ray and DVD players can handle audio discs. Even your Xbox can play them, though the disc drives on Sony PlayStation 4 and 5 consoles weirdly cannot play CDs.

If you need a CD player, the first thing to consider is what kind you want. A personal portable player lets you take your music anywhere. If your record player setup includes a stereo receiver, chances are it has a CD input that you can use to hook up a hi-fi player for at-home listening. This will give you the best audio from your discs. These component players can still be found at big-box retail stores or online music shops like Turntable Lab or RETROSPEKT that specialize in hi-fi systems.

Del Bravo Record Shop, one of the oldest record stores in Texas, has seen an increase in demand for personal CD players that it ships out of its San Antonio store. “They’ve been flying off the shelves,” says Jessica Campa, Del Bravo’s sales associate and social media manager. “We’ve also had about a 12.6 percent increase in CD sales so far this year.”

Bluetooth CD Players are the latest advancement; they let you connect wireless headphones or speakers. If you love the hunt, a thrift store or flea market can be a great place to find a CD player at a great price. Just be sure to test that it works before paying for it. Record stores sometimes keep a variety of used or new CD players as well, depending on their specialty.

The Record Store Is Still Your Friend

Independent record stores are the go-to place to get exclusive vinyl, and many of them still carry CDs. While online shops like Amazon seem like a convenient way to buy these small discs, record stores often receive promotional goodies like posters or stickers that they throw in for free along with your purchase. Oftentimes indie stores will get autographed albums during an artist’s release week to encourage shoppers to come into the store to buy the disc. These are often sold at the regular retail price and not up-charged.

Of course, record stores are great places to buy used discs, and most of the time, the discs are inspected by the staff and you can expect them to play properly and without skips. Stores sometimes even have listening stations so you can preview the used discs.

Track Your Collection

Knowing what music you already have is a great way to prevent accidentally acquiring doubles when you’re out shopping. Thankfully, you don’t need to rely on an Excel spreadsheet. Discogs, an online marketplace and music database for collectors, is well known among vinyl aficionados, but it’s just as helpful as a tool to keep track of your CDs. Not only does the free mobile app feature a barcode scanner that will show you the exact pressing of a CD, it will also show you the current market value of it, in case you come across a rare find in the wild or something that could be overpriced. You can also look up different versions of a CD to find that rare version, like the Japanese pressing with the extra tracks. Discogs will show you a list of the users who own that particular disc who’d be willing to sell it to you for a fair offer.

Inspect Thrifted and Stored CDs

Found that box of old CDs in the garage? Scored a 75-cent copy of Santana’s Abraxas at the thrift store? Be sure to not only check if the disc is actually in the case, but inspect the bottom of the disc—CDs are read by a laser that moves underneath the disc as it spins—for any scratches, discoloration, or spots, which could be a sign of disc rot.

Disc rot is exactly what it sounds like, the deterioration of the reflective layer where a CD’s music data is stored. Sometimes it’s caused by manufacturing defects, but usually it’s the result of improper storage. Over time, heat and humidity can turn these once seemingly indestructible pieces of media into unplayable garbage.

You can score some great finds when thrifting for CDs, but you never know the conditions the discs were stored in before they hit the discount shelf, so learn to spot the most common problems and be discerning. You may even want to bring a portable player with you when you shop so you can test your finds—with the seller’s consent, of course.

Invest in Proper Storage

Similar to a vinyl record, the best way to store a CD is vertically, in its original sleeve, jewel case, or digipack. Any solid shelf makes a good home, but used furniture stores or Goodwill shops will often also have dedicated CD shelving, made of wood or metal, specially designed to fit rows of jewel cases.

About those jewel cases: If they’re damaged or missing pieces, they don’t do as good a job protecting the CDs or artwork inside from spills or scratches. Go the extra step and invest in replacements for cracked jewel cases or damaged interior spindle trays.

If you listen on the move and like to take your discs in the car, a classic CD wallet or CD book is your best solution. You load your disks into the wallet’s plastic pouches and store the jewel case and the artwork somewhere safe, either on the shelf or in a box.

The demand for these nostalgic book-style cases has only increased over the years. “We stocked some recently,” says Steven Alejandro, who has been the general manager at Hogwild Records for over 30 years. “And then the supplier ran out, and now they don’t have any more to sell.”

If you’re lucky to find a case, or you’ve repurposed your parents’ old CD wallets, remember not to leave the case in a hot car, in the sun, or anywhere near a heat source for an extended time.

Keep Your CDs and CD Players Clean

The best way to maintain a physical media collection is to keep everything clean. Found your dream player at a garage sale? Chances are it hasn’t been properly maintained in 20 years. CD players do need to be cleaned every once in a while to ensure the laser lens is free of any debris or fingerprints that can impact playback and audio quality.

On the actual disc, fingerprints, dust, and anything else stuck to the bottom surface can cause audible skips during playback. It's best to use a microfiber cloth and, if necessary, a cleaning solution for extremely dirty CDs. Don’t wipe the disc in a circular motion. Always wipe the disc from the center outward, starting at the hole and pulling the cloth gently toward the outer edge of the disc.

Final Tip

Enjoy your CDs! Rip the contents to your hard drive if you need to, but they sound great when you just give them a spin. There’s a joy in collecting music, because while online streams may be temporary, the physical media we have will always be something we truly own and the actual definition of on-demand.

entries.title: The Best E-Readers That Aren't a Kindle (2026): Kobo, Boox
entries.summary: Want to untether your reading from Amazon? These Kindle alternatives deserve a spot on your nightstand.
entries.content:
Featured in this article

There are no fewer than 10 e-readers in my house at any given time, and I wouldn't have it any other way.

While nothing replaces the feel of a physical book, I usually reach for one of my e-readers as part of my nighttime routine. To me, these tablets are the easiest way to read because they grant immediate access to whatever is in my TBR pile at a given time. Whether it's a library book through the Libby app or a series I'm buying up because I can't wait any longer for a copy to be available, whatever I want to read, I can access it immediately on my e-reader.

It’s also convenient that e-readers (short for “ebook readers”) can store thousands of books at a time. These slim devices use E Ink screens to give text a paperlike appearance. They’re also designed to strain your eyes less than other digital devices, like your phone or computer screen.

And while many strongly associate Kindle with e-reader, you don't have to turn to Amazon for the best device. In fact, my all-around favorite isn't a Kindle at all, and there are plenty of other models to shop from that let you steer clear of the tech behemoth and its recent price increases. These are all my favorite e-readers that won't require you to support Amazon to enjoy the experience.

Updated October 2026: I've moved all Kindle recommendations (and details about the newly announced Kindles) out of our top picks to focus entirely on non-Amazon e-readers. There are also new sections for what I'm testing next and e-reader accessories compatible with my picks.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Comparing Our Favorite E-Readers

Kobo Clara Colour 6 inches, auto-adjusting warm light 300 ppi, black-and-white; 150 ppi, color Yes 16 GB 6 ounces Up to 42 days, USB-C charging

Xteink X4 Pro 4.3 inches, adjustable warm light 219 ppi No 16 GB 2.5 ounces Unspecified battery life, USB-C charging

Honorable Mentions

Below, find a few more e-readers I like but don't necessarily love as much as my top picks.

Boox Go 7 ($270) and Boox Go Color 7 ($290): Boox is known for its wide range of e-paper tablets, including the Boox Go 6 (Gen II) I recommend above. If you're looking for something a little larger with a similar Android-based experience, the Go 7 and Go Color 7 are both solid choices. There are page-turner buttons, and it's a nice square shape that's easy to hold and use. If you, like me, don't use color features a ton, it's worth saving the extra money on the black-and-white model. Regardless, it's great that the price difference between the two models isn't steep.

Boox Palma 2 for $250: This is a fun, pocket-sized device, with fingerprint recognition, a faster CPU, and a newer version of Android than previous models. Former WIRED reviewer Adrienne So loved using it with the Kindle app, but she wishes it cost less. Boox recently announced the Palma 3 is coming out (though it doesn't have a confirmed launch date) which explains why it's been unavailable for so long. The Palma 3 is next on my testing list, but if you want a similar device you can purchase now, the Boox Palma 2 Pro ($400) is available with a higher price tag, but color screen.

Nook GlowLight 4 Plus for $200: The 4 Plus is the only waterproof Nook in the lineup, and it has the biggest screen at 7.8 inches, along with 32 GB of storage. It also has physical page-turn buttons and a headphone jack for listening to audiobooks (you can also connect wireless earbuds via Bluetooth). Unfortunately, it was often slower than my Kindle and tended to freeze. While the large library has cheap and even free ebooks, it's not as good of a selection as Kindle Unlimited. The process of getting a book from the library on a Nook is also frustrating. You'll need to download either Adobe Digital Editions or Android File Transfer before physically connecting the device to your computer and then transferring the files.

Nook 9-inch Lenovo Tablet for $150: If you mainly read cookbooks or other color-intensive materials, and you want a dedicated reader, you might want to consider this affordable tablet from Nook and Lenovo, which has the Nook app built in. It's a tablet rather than an e-paper device like the rest of the gadgets in this guide, so you'll lose the E Ink screen and the distraction-free nature of an e-reader. You can at least turn off notifications while in certain apps, which I recommend doing for the Nook app. It uses Android 13 OS, and it's not built for heavy work, like video or photo editing.

Xteink X4 for $69 and X3 for $69: These are similar to the Xteink X4 Pro above when it comes to the app and basic capabilities, but you'll lose out on the touchscreen, home button, and front light. Instead, there are more buttons, providing a Tamagotchi-like experience as you tap them to go back and forth between menus and pages of your reading material. The X3 is super small, with just a 3.7-inch screen that fits on the back of my iPhone 16 Pro, and it has stronger magnets to put itself into place. But the standard X4 is more comfortable to read on than the X3 since it's larger (and won't require quite as many page turns, though it'll still need a lot) with a 4.3-inch screen, like the X4 Pro above.

What I’m Testing Next

There have been several new e-readers announced, mainly new models from Boox like the Palma 3 and Picco, that I'll be reading my latest books on this fall, which will include R.F. Kuang's Babel and the latest ACOTAR book, along with an alarmingly long list of suspended holds in my Libby app that I really need to work on. Here's what I'll be testing next:

Boox Palma 3 for $320: Boox's popular Palma devices are made to be mobile e-paper screens, and are a popular choice as a smaller e-reader. The new Palma 3 has been announced after months of the Palma 2 being out of stock, and it promises a 6.13-inch screen, dual-tone front light, a rear camera, dual microphones, and a customizable smart button. There's no timeline yet for its launch, but I'm hoping we see it available before the end of the year.

Boox Picco for $100: This miniature e-reader will have a tiny 3.97-inch screen and be Boox's smallest e-reader to date. The Boox Picco isn't the smallest e-reader ever—Xteink still holds that crown—but promises a different experience to Boox's other e-readers and e-paper devices by focusing on Boox's new Tiles app and productivity tools. Boox says it's the first of its Tiles ecosystem, so I'm keeping an eye out for more launches within that line. The Picco is currently available for preorder and is due to ship in October.

Boox Note Mini C for $550: When Boox announced the Palma 3, it also announced its new e-paper tablet, the Boox Note Air6 C, and a miniaturized version, the Boox Note Mini C. The Mini C has a smaller 8.52-inch screen that's more ideal for reading than the larger tablet, and I'm curious how it compares to both the Palma 3 and the Boox Go line.

The 2026 Kindles: Amazon has announced new versions of all three of its main e-readers, with a 2026 version of Kindle ($150), Kindle Paperwhite ($200), and Kindle Colorsoft ($290) coming out this fall, plus a Kids version ($180+) of each of these new models. There are now aluminum-backed versions of all three, though the Paperwhite and Colorsoft have it as part of the higher-end Signature Edition that comes with a few more features. I'll be testing and will add my top pick to this guide for reference, but this guide will focus more on non-Kindle e-readers going forward.

What If I Want a Kindle?

Maybe you've read this guide and decided a Kindle is best for you. That's fine! Kindle is my longest-used ecosystem and it's plenty convenient, especially if you already have ebooks purchased through Amazon. While I have an entire guide dedicated to shopping for a Kindle, here's a quick overview of my top picks (and other models you might spot).

Also, Kindle does have new versions of the base Kindle, Kindle Paperwhite, Kindle Colorsoft, and its Kids versions of each model coming out. You might want to wait and see if you prefer the newest versions to these, and I'll be testing them soon to see how they compare to past Kindles and other e-readers. Kindle also raised the prices of most of its e-readers at the end of August, and the new models match that pricing.

Kindle Colorsoft Signature for $320 and Kindle Colorsoft ($290): The Kindle Colorsoft Signature is Amazon's first Kindle with a color screen. I do like the Colorsoft if you read books with illustrations or heavily annotate your e-books, but the Kobo devices I recommend can do the same thing for cheaper.

Kindle Scribe (3rd Gen, 2025) for $500 and Kindle Scribe Colorsoft for $630: The latest Kindle Scribe arrived in December 2025 with a color version. It also has a new exterior design that does away with the single thicker side and standardizes bezels and frames across all sizes, and a lot of AI features. The older Kindle Scribe (2nd Gen) is still my preferred option if you want a Kindle e-reader that doubles as a digital notebook.

Kindle Scribe Without Front Light for $430: This is the third and final installment of Amazon's latest generation of Kindle Scribes. It's similar to the third-gen Kindle Scribe above, but it removes the front light and wireless charging. If you want a cheaper Kindle Scribe, I still prefer the second-generation model, though you'll lose out on AI reading features and the ability to connect to Google Drive and Microsoft OneDrive.

Great E-Reader Accessories

Looking to jazz up your new e-reader? Here are some of my favorite accessories to pair with my favorite non-Kindle e-readers. It's a tougher buy to find—since Kindles are so popular, most cases and accessories are made with those models in mind, but there are options out there for the rest of the e-reader world, too. Here's what I've tested and liked for my e-readers.

FAQs

How Do You Get Ebooks?

Ebooks can be cheap, but as with regular books, the cost can add up if you're a big reader. To keep costs low, take advantage of your library card and check out ebooks instantly from the comfort of your home. We have a detailed guide that explains How to Get Free Kindle Books With Your Library Card, but the short version is that most libraries distribute books via OverDrive. You can access these books a few ways: through Kindle or directly from OverDrive with a Kobo, or you can download the Libby app. These ebooks are automatically removed from your device and returned to the library when they're due.

Each e-reader's own book service varies in quality. My favorite is Kindle Unlimited for $12 a month, which includes millions of titles, including audiobooks and magazines. Amazon's Prime Reading also offers a handful of free books every month, which is good to know if you already have a Prime account. You can even lend books to friends and family for a short while (or have them share a book with you). For more details on each option, check out our guide to the Best Ebook Subscription Services here.

What File Formats Do E-Readers Support?

The most widely used format is EPUB, which works natively with all the e-readers in this guide except for Kindle—technically. You can still upload EPUB files to your Kindle, but you'll have to use the “Send to Kindle” feature (through Amazon, your email, or the Kindle app) to convert it to Amazon's proprietary format called AZW. (Newer Kindles support AZW3 and KFX, specifically). Other formats that will work with these e-readers include PDF, TXT, HTML, DOC, and DOCX.

Can I Install Apps on an E-Reader?

Kindle, Kobo, and Nook all use proprietary operating systems that don't allow you to install third-party apps. The Boox, on the other hand, runs Android (mainly Android 11 and newer). That means you can use it to download any apps available in the Google Play Store or side-load apps from your computer.

Do You Need an E-Reader? What About a Phone or Tablet?

You don't have to buy a separate device to read ebooks. Smartphones and tablets are perfect for this purpose. You can use Amazon's Kindle app to read ebooks (iOS, Android) and download OverDrive's Libby app (iOS, Android) for library-book access. However, the E Ink screens found in e-readers are just nicer to look at. I also like that these devices are one-trick ponies; there are no distracting notifications or social media feeds ripe for doomscrolling.

If you'd still rather have one smart device you can use for reading and other purposes, take a look at our Best Tablets and Best iPads guides for recommendations.

What About a Digital Notebook?

I've tried just about every digital notebook on the market; these devices are designed for handwritten notes on an E Ink screen. E-readers with that capability usually still prioritize reading, though there are plenty of models I like that can do both. The Kobo Libra Colour is my favorite option for annotating books, and it can double as a small digital notebook. If you want a larger option, check out my full guide to every digital notebook I've tested.

How Do I Test E-Readers?

The most important step I take when testing e-readers is to read on them! I spend hours reading books acquired in a variety of formats, including books I purchased directly from each brand's store, downloaded from local libraries via OverDrive/Libby, and PDFs acquired for free from God knows where.

In the process, I evaluate battery life, brightness, performance lag, screen responsiveness, and text sharpness. I check for extra tools, like whether the tablet in question accommodates accessories like a stylus. I also note features like waterproofing, annotation capability, and access to exclusive subscription services.

entries.title: Best Mosquito Repellents for Your Yard: What Works and What Doesn’t (2026)
entries.summary: After years of testing repellents, traps, and sprays, I found a few ways to keep the bugs at bay—and plenty that aren’t worth the effort.
entries.content:
Mosquitoes suck. Literally, figuratively, and every other way. These bloodsuckers have been a worldwide menace since the beginning of recorded history. A popularly reposted infographic lists them as—by far—the world’s deadliest animal, thanks to the parade of nasty diseases they can transmit. West Nile, Zika, chikungunya, malaria, dengue—these are no longer illnesses confined to the global south. In recent years, all have been discovered in bugs in the United States.

Ridding your property of mosquitoes is a decidedly Quixotic effort. You can stem the tide for a while, but you can’t ever win the war. Once whatever abatement method you use has worn off, they swoop back in, thirstier than ever. Nevertheless, you have to do something. Left unattended, mosquitoes can quickly turn from a nuisance to an epidemic that makes your outdoor space completely unusable.

Outside of wide-scale community mosquito spraying programs, most personal and home-based mosquito abatement tools focus on repelling them rather than trying to outright kill them. Insecticides like DEET work by being rubbed onto the skin, while metofluthrin and allethrin work in vapor form, creating a cloud of repellent that works without you having to make physical contact with the chemicals. Trapping mosquitoes is another potential option, luring them into a chamber from which they can’t escape.

For years I’ve tried innumerable technologies and tactics to rid my property—and my very susceptible skin—from mosquitoes. Here’s what I’ve uncovered to date that works—and what doesn’t.

Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.

Featured Products

Best Personal Repellent Gear

This pint-sized repeller weighs a little more than a pound and recharges via a USB-C cable. Power it up and a heating element inside warms a vial of metofluthrin, releasing mosquito-repulsing vapor in your immediate vicinity, about 10 feet in every direction. It’s simple and extremely portable, making it easy to move from one area to another.

The system works. It warms up in just a few minutes and effectively keeps bugs at bay, provided you keep the repeller close by. Best of all, I was able to take it with me as I moved around the yard—but be warned, there’s some lag time for the vapor cloud to reform each time you relocate. A small chemical replacement cartridge lasts for about 36 hours; refills are $39 for a 2-pack.

Note that Thermacell markets myriad versions of this product, including a unit with a built-in light, one with a docking station for easier charging, one with longer battery life, and one that is ruggedized and can be worn around the neck on a lanyard. Any of the above will get the job done (and done well) in functionally the same way.

This butane-powered device offers a twist on the E-ZoneGuard line, containing no battery at all, which may be preferred in some exceptionally off-the-grid environments. Instead, a butane cartridge twists into the system. When activated (no flame needed), it heats up a replaceable chemical mat that slides into a groove on top of the device, this one using allethrin instead of metofluthrin. One downside: The vapor shield promised by the Fuel-Zoneguard stretches only about 7½ feet in each direction, more restrictive than the E-Zoneguard, and a butane canister will only get you about 12 hours of operation. Allethrin may also be less effective than metofluthrin against pests. That said, I experienced great results with this product and found the freedom from cables to be liberating. Refills run $19 for 24 hours of extra fuel and insecticide mats (sold together).

The Fuel-Zoneguard is also sold as part of a lantern or in a handheld form, designed for use on the go. (As with E-Zoneguard products, the underlying technology is identical.)

Best Large-Scale Repellent Gear

Take Thermacell’s E-Zoneguard system and make it yard-sized, and you’ve got LIV, a semi-permanent solution that uses the same repellent chemical (metofluthrin) but dramatically expands its coverage potential.

The system is built around a hub that plugs into wall power and connects to your home’s Wi-Fi. Up to 10 freestanding repellers connect to this hub via cables. You string them in a chain to surround your deck, your pool, or whatever else you want to protect from mosquitoes. Arranged in a rough circle, the resultant cloud of repellent serves as a large-scale barrier that can protect the whole family from being attacked. It’s all controlled via a mobile app (with Alexa support allegedly in the works), so you can fire the system up before you even head outside.

It’s one of the most effective systems I’ve tested, in large part because it pumps out so much repellent at precise locations. While nothing is perfect, LIV is about as close as it gets, protecting my entire swimming pool and deck at the touch of a button on its mobile app.

The only catch is that LIV is far from inexpensive, and Thermacell no longer sells it as a DIY solution; you’ll need a professional installer to complete the job. If saving your skin (and potentially your health) from mosquitoes is important to you, it could be worth it.

Tiki BiteFighter—from the company that makes the iconic torches—is an ingenious twist on the wider-scale repellent concept that takes advantage of wiring you may already have. The system works with string lights: Just remove a bulb from your lights and screw the Plug & Repel into the socket. When the lights are on, the device heats up a vial of metofluthrin that attaches to the bottom of the repellent unit, protecting the immediate vicinity from mosquitoes. (In theory, you can also use it with any overhead light socket.)

Naturally, the device comes with some caveats. The biggest is that it requires a (standard size) E26 socket to connect to; many string lights, including mine, use much smaller E12 candelabra bulbs, so compatibility can be a problem. Second, the range of BiteFighter’s vapor is considerably smaller than Thermacell’s: Tiki recommends plugging in a repeller every 12 feet. That can require a significant investment in hardware, mar your lighting aesthetic, and require lots of maintenance. (The system ships with a 12-hour metofluthrin pod; 48-hour replacement pods cost $10 each.)

Still, if you have the right environment, with compatible string lights surrounding or criss-crossing your outdoor space, the solution is much more affordable than a hard-wired system like LIV. If you only plan to use the system occasionally, the math is even more compelling.

Just OK: Mosquito Traps

These devices may look like old-school bug zappers, but they’re actually traps, designed to lure bugs in with a purple light, then sequester them in a chamber thanks to the tiny fan that sucks them in. Mosqitter's and Dynatrap’s devices work almost exactly the same way, boasting coverage that spans up to an acre, depending on the model you choose.

I tried both of these products—in Mosqitter’s case for months, letting it run all summer long—and found that while they were both effective at capturing insects, neither one attracted many mosquitoes. In both cases, I returned after a few weeks to find the trap chamber filled almost exclusively with moths. I don’t really love moths, either, but I don’t feel like I need to go out of my way to kill them.

I spoke to Mosqitter about my results and they suggested adding a packet of mosquito attractant to the device ($25, lasts a month), but this didn’t have any result on my mosquito catch rate. Again, mostly moths at the end of the testing period.

So, why am I saying these might be worth a try? As Mosqitter pointed out to me, there are countless species of mosquitoes—3200 globally, 174 in the US—and they don’t all behave the same. The ones around Austin may be resistant to the attractant and blasé about purple light, instead preferring to dine exclusively on human flesh. (This certainly tracks.) So while my results were lackluster, I’m willing to concede that users in other parts of the world, where the bugs are less hearty, may have better luck with it. If you don’t get good results, you can always return the gear for a refund.

If You Do Get Stung

Less effective

I’ve tried plenty of products that promise to kill or repel mosquitoes. These have not been effective—or, at least, not worth the money and effort involved.

This oddity arrives as a plastic bucket that you fill partway with water, mimicking a mosquito breeding site. A chemical-laced band hovers over this water, slowly contaminating it with a poison that kills adult mosquitoes and their eggs. The band must be replaced monthly. I tested this system for two months but found that the water evaporated much too quickly and, more importantly, the whole thing became an attractant for mammalian wildlife like racoons and opossums, which periodically tossed it around, maybe in the hopes of getting at the water. It’s a cheap option at $35, but not something I was keen to leave on my patio long-term.

The lowest of low-tech anti-mosquito solutions, Mosquito Dunks are small discs that you can drop into any amount of standing water, either natural (water feature like a fountain) or man-made (a bucket you intentionally fill with water as a trap). These contain a bacteria that’s toxic to mosquitoes but won’t hurt other wildlife, slowly releasing into the water as they dissolve over the course of a month. The only problem: They smell awful, and of course you need a reliable source of standing water for them to work at all. That’s fine if you have a handy pond that you don’t want to drain. Much less exciting in the average backyard.

$100/treatment and up

If you live in mosquito country, chances are your neighborhood is teeming with companies that promise to repel the bugs by spraying chemicals into the trees and foliage around your property, warding them off. I paid for a service to spray my property for years, and found that a very familiar routine developed: Immediately after each spray, my yard would be almost devoid of bugs, and my family would have two or three days of bite-free bliss. After that, the spray would wear off and the bugs would return, leaving us another 18 days or so until the next triweekly treatment. (Any amount of rain would also wash away all of the treatment chemicals even quicker.) Given the cost of over $2,000 per year, I’ve never been happier with a decision to cancel a service.

Mosquitoes just aren’t attracted to shiny lights the way other insects are. You’ll hear plenty of satisfying pops if you hang a bug zapper near your pool, but you won’t likely find many of the dead to be mosquitoes. Skip ’em.

entries.title: A Decade-Long Experiment Is Unlocking the Mysteries of the Ocean’s ‘Deep Reefs’
entries.summary: Scientists left structures up to 100 meters under the surface. Here’s what they found when they retrieved them 10 years later.
entries.content:
This story originally appeared on Vox and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

On a bright, sunny day last May, I stood on a boat surrounded by the turquoise waters of the island nation of Palau. I was there in the western Pacific watching scuba divers as they prepared to bring up evidence of a mysterious aquatic world.

Palau is famous for its spectacular and rich coral reefs. But these divers were planning to descend past those sun-lit marine communities and down into a lesser-known twilight zone known as the “mesophotic coral ecosystem.”

Mesophotic essentially means “middle” and “light,” which is where these ecosystems are—not quite in the bright daylight, not quite in the profound darkness, but somewhere in between. For simplicity’s sake, we’ll call these communities, which range from some 30 meters to 150 meters below the surface, the “deep reefs.”

One of the divers on the boat with me was a zoologist and curator at the California Academy of Sciences named Luiz Rocha, who has spent decades studying these deep reefs and their secrets.

“Anything between 30 meters and 150 meters is really, really unknown,” he told me.

Because these deep reefs are so unknown, researchers like Rocha are left with big questions. They want to get a baseline picture of what is going on in these ecosystems—even just who lives there!—so that they can better understand how they function. They’ve also tried to work out whether (or not) these deep reefs might provide a refuge for species living in shallower coral reefs.

I was in Palau for Vox’s Unexplainable podcast because, in an effort to gather more information about these mysterious places, Rocha left some scientific structures down in these twilight depths back in 2016. Those structures then spent almost a decade becoming encrusted with all kinds of marine life. And now, Rocha was back to retrieve them, hoping that he—along with many other scientists — would be able to open them up, like a box of scientific puzzle pieces, full of clues about this under-understood marine world.

One thing that’s often acknowledged in papers about mesophotic coral ecosystems is that scientists don’t know as much as they’d like to. A National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration article about them from 2019 is full of “mays,” as in: They may “serve as essential fish habitat for economically and ecologically important species.

Researchers do know some things, of course. They know that these deep reefs can be found in many of the same regions as shallower coral reefs—so mainly the tropical and subtropical parts of the world, like Micronesia, the Caribbean, and even the Gulf of Mexico. They’ve found that there are many species that seem to be unique to these places, and recent research points to their potential susceptibility to climate change.

Researchers have also gotten a sense of some of the key differences between these deep reefs and their shallower coral neighbors. In shallow reefs, hard corals team up with photosynthesizing algae. The algae provide the corals with nutrients, and the corals secrete a calcium-carbonate matrix that helps create the architecture of the reef.

As you go deeper, though, the light begins to fade, and the opportunities for photosynthesis start to fade with it. The temperature also drops. So the animals living down in the deep reefs are ones that can survive in a dimmer, cooler world.

Scientists can dive into the deep reefs to try to learn more about these understudied places—as Rocha has—but exploring down at 100 meters requires more difficult, riskier technical diving than exploring at shallower depths. The deeper you dive, for example, the faster gases get pushed into your tissues, which imposes limits on these really deep dives.

“We have a very, very short time,” Rocha says, “And by short time, I mean five minutes. Six, seven minutes.”

Scientists can take some pictures in that time, make some measurements, or collect a few samples, but then they have to move back upwards—a process that can take hours, since they must rise slowly to avoid decompression sickness.

It is, obviously, not particularly efficient to study an ecosystem in five- to seven-minute intervals. People have also used remote-operated vehicles and submersibles to explore the deep reefs, but those have their own issues, and cameras can’t always capture all the detail you might want, or photograph more secretive, cryptic animals. So huge gaps remain in scientific knowledge about these ecosystems.

“Whenever we go somewhere,” Rocha says, “the first thing we find is new species. It’s the most basic thing in science you can do.” But this effort goes beyond just cataloging new species of fish, sponges, or sea slugs.

Rocha wants to answer fundamental questions like: What is the main energy source for everything down here in the dim light? What does the food chain look like? How have things evolved to live at these depths? How similar are they to the shallow ecosystems, and how different? How are they affected by climate change—and what’s the most efficient way to protect them?

But Rocha says that “in some ways, we don’t even know what questions to ask. We really only know what the crucial questions are when we have a baseline understanding of the ecosystem. And for deep reefs, we don’t have that yet.”

Rocha is not deterred by the enormous number of question marks that surround these deep reefs. For years now, he has been gathering bits of basic information about them, often via those very short dives.

About a decade ago, though, Rocha got interested in another method for sampling the biodiversity of this sort of marine ecosystem—a technique involving “autonomous reef monitoring structures” or ARMS.

Basically, each ARMS is a stack of several PVC plates, separated at uniform intervals and attached to a base plate. They look like little gray, featureless hotels. You take them to a place that you want to study, bring them down, secure them, and then leave them alone for a while to let them collect … life.

“As soon as you drop any kind of clean structure on a reef,” Rocha says, “it starts getting colonized by larvae of everything around it—of sponges, gorgonians, corals. And then, because there’s a lot of hiding spots between the plates—so between the floors of the hotel—they start getting colonized by shrimp, by mollusks, by ascidians, by anything you can imagine in the ocean. And it becomes this stable, diverse mini reef, if you will, packed with a lot of biodiversity that would be very hard to collect all at once in any given reef.”

A few years after that initial drop, you come back, collect the ARMS, and then study the mini reef that has grown on them. You can sample and touch and analyze things to your heart’s content.

It’s not only a very effective way to collect lots of creatures, all at once, but also a great way to do so in a standardized way. If you went down—or sent a robot down—to collect an encrusted rock from a reef, you could learn a lot about the life on it, but it would be hard to compare the life on that rock to life on other rocks from other reefs, or even the same reef, because each rock would have its own unique characteristics. Not so for ARMS.

“ Every one’s the same,” Chris Meyer, director of the Smithsonian Global ARMS program, told me. “It’s prefab housing, and then you just look to see who moves in.”

To Rocha, this seemed like a great way to get a really good, long look at the deep reefs instead of the brief glimpses he was getting from diving. It was also, he told me, fairly cheap to deploy them. So from 2016 to 2018, with some private funding, he and his colleagues left ARMS in some of the deep reefs around Palau—as well as in Guam, the Marshall Islands, and French Polynesia. They installed some around 50 meters, and some around 100, and then some around 10 meters, so he could compare the deep reefs to their shallower neighbors.

After that, he waited.

In fact, he waited a little longer than he would have liked, because the retrieval of ARMS is more expensive than deploying them, so he had to work out more funding.

Eventually, private funders agreed to underwrite the retrieval of the ARMS that Rocha had left. Which is how he and his fellow divers finally found themselves on a boat in Palau again, ready to pull up these structures from the deep.

Over the course of a few days, I watched a whole team of people pull several ARMS out of the deep reefs of Palau. Some of the ARMS were relatively sparse, but others were almost fuzzy with organisms—vibrant with red and orange and green and pink and white. One had a massive sponge attached to it; another had several delicate fronds dangling from it like coralline ferns. The ARMS collected each day traveled to the Palau International Coral Reef Center in bins full of seawater, where the scientists quickly got to work—seeing and touching (and smelling) this mysterious ecosystem right up close.

The process was, as it turned out, equal parts magical excitement and well-oiled, Cheez-It–fueled disassembly line. After the plates were taken apart, Meyer took photographs of the plates—what he called a “time capsule of the place.” Others in the lab picked carefully through trays of debris, hunting for tiny crabs and worms and mollusks, or scraped samples off the plates and deposited them in tubes.

They collected sea squirts, said to be our closest invertebrate relatives. They collected sponges—flat ones that felt dry underwater, thick ones with bristles like tiny, unmoving caterpillars, one as thin as a flake of skin and shot through with silver filaments. They collected strange, soft corals known as octocorals, and they collected colonies of animals called bryozoans, which created what looked like swirling, two-dimensional honeycombs.

“We’re looking for every unique thing, which we call a morphospecies,” a Smithsonian research biologist named Sarah Tweedt explained. “And we’re trying to get some representative tissue samples from all of these things so that we can sequence the DNA—and match the DNA to the organism.”

That is, of course, assuming there is already a known genetic match in our existing DNA libraries.

On the first day that I spent with the team, a Cal Academy curator named Terry Goslinger identified several potential new species. He is an expert on colorful, delightful sea slugs known as nudibranchs, and so, because of his deep knowledge (and because nudibranchs’ bright hues and patterns make them somewhat easier to tell apart than some other underwater creatures), he was able to make some on-the-spot calls about whether or not certain species were likely to be new to science, pending genetic testing to confirm.

Many of the animals were trickier to pin down, though. The researchers did their best to identify the creatures they were finding, but even now, several months out, there’s still a lot of work to be done. Of the close to 3,000 specimens, only a small fraction were identified at a species level. The numbers are a little bit inexact because researchers are still processing the data, but when I checked in with a Cal Academy postdoc working on the project, Susanne Bähr, in July, she told me that only 3 percent of samples had been ID’d by species, and a little less than 20 had a genus designation. Many, many more were only identified at higher, broader taxonomic levels. Genetic testing of the samples, paired with photographs and descriptions of the samples, will help people work out more specific species, and also help them identify whether certain species are new to science.

The most important parts of this work will involve more than just identifying species. In fact, the more time I spent with these researchers in the lab (including one evening spent with them as they worked past midnight), the more I got the sense that, while they seemed excited about seeing new species, they seemed equally excited to witness relationships between animals.

When I walked into the lab one day, for example, several people urged me to go over and look through a microscope at a creature known as a pompom crab—a tiny yellow crustacean holding purple anemones in its modified front claws. Tweedt was extremely jazzed when she found something referred to as a “skeleton shrimp,” which looked to me like the marine equivalent of a stick insect, blending in on something called a hydroid. She pulled me aside another time, around 1 in the morning, to show me “the frosting on the cake” of the day, which turned out to be some bright red sea snails and the bright red octocorals they seemed to live on

As she put it in a later conversation, these relationships are, in many ways, the key takeaway from this ARMS project, and what distinguishes it from efforts to bring up a few individual samples at a time. Studying them, or even just looking at the fuller picture ARMS provide, is what will let researchers tackle some of the outstanding questions about these ecosystems. Bähr, for example, is already working with the data from ARMS retrieved in Guam, trying to analyze how much overlap (or lack thereof) there is between species at different depths in the deep reefs.

Really, though, this is all just the beginning. In one of our conversations, Rocha compared the work they are doing now to ecology work done in the mid-20th century to understand how species’ vertical distribution changes as you go up a mountain. This drove home for me how far behind researchers working on the mesophotic deep reefs are compared to their colleagues working on, say, shallower coral reefs. I asked him what kept him working on such a difficult puzzle.

“It’s the reward at the end of it,” he said. “If it’s a hard puzzle, at the end of it, the reward is always bigger.”

“But in our lifetimes, will we assemble the deep reef puzzle?” I asked.

“No, we will not assemble the puzzle, no,” Rocha said, “but we’ll generate some good pieces for the next generation to assemble.”

entries.title: 20% Off Brooks Promo Code | October 2026
entries.summary: Enjoy 20% off your first order with a Brooks coupon code, plus top discounts and deals on our favorite Brooks running shoes.
entries.content:
What if I told you Brooks Running started out making ballet slippers and bathing shoes? Founded in 1914, the Seattle-based company spent decades making just about everything except running shoes, moving from baseball cleats to roller skates, football cleats, children’s shoes, and softball cleats. It wasn’t until 1972 that Brooks made running its focus, and the company has been refining the category ever since.

Brooks introduced one of the industry’s earliest uses of EVA foam, developed the first running shoe with a breathable GORE-TEX upper, and introduced the Kinetic Wedge, an innovative design tailored to women’s anatomy.

So, while Brooks may not be the trendiest brand, it has built a reputation for dependable support, comfort, and durability. Here at WIRED, Brooks has plenty of fans, especially for trail and gravel running. The company also offers apparel we regularly recommend, including sports bras, outerwear, and running bottoms.

Brooks Running shoes are reasonably priced for performance running footwear, with many models hovering around $150. If you’re in the market for a new pair, I’ve rounded up the best Brooks Running promo codes and coupons worth checking out.

Score 20% Off Your First Order With Brooks Promo Code

If you’ve never ordered from Brooks’ website before, new customers get 20% off their first order after subscribing to email. You can apply the one-time Brooks coupon code to top-selling shoes, like the Caldera 7 and Adrenaline shoes, as well as other gear and apparel. It’s an easy way to save on some of their top products and take your road and trail running game to the next level.

More Brooks Coupons and Offers

Are you already a member of Brooks Run Club? If you sign up, you get member perks like early access to sales, free standard shipping with no order minimum, and free express shipping on orders from Brooks. Membership also includes more runner-specific perks, such as a free birthday gift and the chance to earn prizes by syncing your fitness tracker and contributing research to the Brooks team. You can also win a chance to visit the Seattle flagship store and have your gait analyzed by Brooks’ team. To join, visit Brooks Run Club and register using the Brooks promo code.

If you shop and buy a complete outfit in one transaction from one of Brooks’ recommended buying guides—like Warm Weather Running Outfits or Fall Weather Running Outfits—you can get 15% off automatically applied at checkout. This is a fantastic deal if you only just realized in the past 10 days that you’ve been running in hail in your tiny shorts and cropped sports bra.

Save on Our Favorite Brooks Running Shoes

Brooks makes so many iconic running shoes that it’s hard to list them all. I’m currently running in the Brooks Glycerin Max, which is one of the cushiest shoes I’ve ever tried. I don’t feel particularly stable on uneven terrain, but the padding is noticeably springy and cushy if you’ve been putting in some serious miles. WIRED director Michael Calore is a fan of the Brooks Ghost line, and if you’re planning to hit the trails in the cold, wet Pacific Northwest, I’d suggest the Brooks Cascadia Gore-Tex. The Adrenaline is the company’s most popular shoe.

Preorder Your Favorite Glycerin Now

One of the most anticipated Brooks drops is the Glycerin line. These shoes are built to be durable while allowing freedom of movement and flexibility. The cushioned shoes are comfortable for running and movement on many types of terrain. Many shoes in the Glycerin line are available to pre-order, including the Glycerin Flex, Glycerin 23, and Glycerin GTS 23. Be sure to check out the Glycerin line to see which is best for you.

The Cascadia Elite Available Now

Brooks is constantly dropping new shoe styles, ensuring there’s a shoe for every runner. The new Cascadia Elite Brooks Running shoe is unisex and great for trail running, with PEBA cushioning, a Vibram Megagrip Elite outsole, and a MATRYX engineered woven upper with Kevlar fibers to help secure your feet firmly, no matter what terrain you’re traversing. This shoe has light, springy cushioning that helps propel you forward, whether that’s competitive trail racing, Sub-ultras, VKs, or ultras.

Upcoming Brooks Sale Events to Watch Out For

Do you have a runner in your life? The odds are they’re taking stock of their winter apparel and shoes, deciding whether these leggings will make it through another winter. The best time to save is during seasonal sales, with discounts on footwear and apparel, including popular items like the Ghost 16 running shoes.

Do you have running military, nurses, or first responders in your life? Brooks Running also offers 25% off full-priced items for verified community heroes with a Brooks promo code. Sign up here.

Brooks Discount: Shop Pre-Owned Shoes at Brooks

If you’re looking for a new pair of shoes but don’t have the cash to invest in a brand-new, high-end pair, look no further than Brooks’ restock page, where gently used Brooks shoes are on sale at deeply discounted prices. They have both men’s and women’s sections, recently added shoes, and a breakdown of bestselling styles, including the Adrenaline, Ghost, Glycerin, and Hyperion.

Brooks Coupon: 20% Off Join the Brooks Run Club

If you’re looking to shop at Brooks, it’s a great idea to join the Brooks Run Club for additional perks and discounts. Some of the best benefits Run Club offers include a 20% discount on apparel when you join and an annual birthday gift. You’ll just need to log in or join the club to get the discount code.

Brooks Sports Medicine Ambassador Program: 40% Off

If you’re a sports medicine professional, you can save big and get rewarded at Brooks Running. The Brooks Sports Medicine Ambassador Program is a free membership for eligible sports medicine professionals, a way to say thank you for the care they provide to runners and athletes. All you have to do is verify your status by signing in or creating an ID.me account to confirm your qualifications. Then, you’ll get a steep 40% discount on the first $1,000 spent on eligible items in Brooks Running online orders (it resets every January 1).

Brooks Return Policy and 90 Day Wear Test

Brooks knows how important gear is to athletes. So, you can take your Brooks gear for a 90-day trial run, and if you aren't satisfied, return it for free. If you’re at all unsatisfied with your Brooks purchase, you can return it for free with no shipping or restocking fees.

Does Brooks Running Offer Free Shipping?

For Brooks Run Club members, shipping is free! Free shipping applies to standard shipping, including PO Box and US Territories, which takes about 5 to 8 business days. For members, express and next-day delivery is discounted to $25 or $15, unless the total is over $160, in which case express is free. Non-members pay an additional $5 for all shipping options.

entries.summary: Explore today’s top DoorDash promo codes for $25 off your first order, free delivery, and 50% off DashPass for students and select users.
entries.content:
What can I say about DoorDash to truly capture what this company means to me? I could say it’s the father I never had; it’s the mother I’ve always wanted; the warm embrace of a friend you haven’t seen in a while; the sound of rain as you fall asleep… One of the greatest inventions of the 21st century is the ability to have virtually any food you crave delivered to your front door without getting up or even speaking to another human. We’ve rounded up the best verified DoorDash promo codes, special offers, and free delivery deals.

DoorDash Promo Codes for New Users in 2026

Enjoy staying at home and having your meals delivered. Currently, you can save $8 on orders of $25 or more at participating restaurants. Additionally, there's a DoorDash promo code that offers up to $25 off your first order of $30 or more. You can also receive 25% off your first alcohol delivery via DoorDash. Remember to use the promo code USDASHTRIAL2Q26 for the best savings.

Save up to $35 With DoorDash Coupons and This Week’s Deals

Beyond using the DoorDash promo codes above, you can save more with rotating weekly deals–plus these special offers. The best coupons include 25% off your entire order, $5 off $20, and 30% off lunchtime delivery. Unlike many promo codes reserved for new customers, existing customers can score too and save 30% (up to $8) for a limited time. Now you have the perfect excuse to get your munch on.

There are also great BOGO deals (who doesn’t love a buy-one-get-one moment?) like buy 1 get 1 free entrees and a free appetizer when you spend $15 or more, up to $35 off. While discount codes are often only available for your first order, both new and existing customers can take advantage of these coupons. Keep the Deals section in mind to save big with limited-time offers based on your delivery location.

Get 15% Off DoorDash With Our WIRED Code

With this exclusive WIRED DoorDash promo code, first-time customers can get 15% off their first order placed through DoorDash, with savings up to $10 on a $15 minimum order using DoorDash coupon code USEG15OFF2Q26. This DoorDash promo code is only applicable to new customers and cannot be applied toward alcohol orders.

DoorDash Online Coupons

Depending on your location, you can get personalized DoorDash coupons and promo codes, along with local favorites, so you can save while revisiting old favorites and exploring new hot spots. There are literally hundreds of top DoorDash promos and new offers that rotate daily for local restaurants, grocery stores, and more. Plus, with DoorDash, you’ll get a $0 delivery fee on eligible orders, free items and discounts on food, deals on groceries, and DashPass member-exclusive offers. When I entered my ZIP code, I discovered [DoorDash deals](https://www.doordash.com/en-US/promos) for things like 20% off orders, $5 discounts, and free items at new restaurants I’d never heard of before (my potential new faves?).

Score Free Delivery on Your Next DoorDash Order

DoorDash is the answer to 21st-century America's laziness and was a godsend during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, when customers could get their favorite foods from restaurants, groceries, and household products delivered right to their door without leaving the safety of their couch. If you’re more of an Uber Eats person and haven’t signed up for DoorDash, now is a great time to sign up and get a $0 delivery fee on your first order. Whether you want a romantic night in with your favorite sushi spot across town or are having a pounding headache early Sunday morning and in desperate need of Advil and Pedialyte from the gas station up the road (not speaking from personal experience or anything), DoorDash has you covered. Go ahead, stay in bed.

DoorDash Student Discount: 50% Off DashPass

Once you’ve signed up and received free delivery on your first order, there are still more ways to save. DoorDash offers a student discount, allowing students to get 50% off a DashPass account. DashPass is a subscription that provides unlimited deliveries from 1,000s of eligible restaurants with $0 delivery fees. To sign up for student DashPass, simply verify your student status with Sheer ID. The student DashPass Plan is half off the regular DashPass Plans, priced at $4.99 a month or $48 annually.

Get 50% Off and 3 Months of DashPass Free

If you’re not a student, don’t worry. There are tons of other great discounts available on DoorDash. Sign up for DashPass to get $0 delivery fees on orders, 5% back on pickup orders, and tons of other benefits.

If you bank at Chase, Chase card members are eligible for exclusive DashPass benefits on DoorDash and Caviar when an eligible Chase credit card is added to their account. Chase is offering 3 months of DashPass free, plus 50% off the next 9 months of service.

Whether you're looking for tried-and-true chains for burgers and pizza like McDonald’s, Shake Shack, or Domino’s, or authentic Mexican like Chipotle or Taco Bell (I kid! Don’t come for me), DoorDash is a great way to eat your way around the world without ever leaving your couch.

DoorDash Delivery Updates and New Features in 2026

DoorDash has some exciting updates, including the launch of its Going Out program, a new dine-in program for customers that will start in NYC and Miami. With this program, diners can book restaurant reservations directly through the DoorDash app and will be rewarded for their loyalty with exclusive offers when dining in, as well as rewards for regular visits to favorite spots. Plus, DashPass members will get even more exclusive perks and in-store rewards. Check it out for yourself—explore the new “Going Out” tab in the DoorDash app, redeem exclusive in-store offers, and earn rewards for repeat visits. Customers save an average of $9 when using these perks.

DoorDash is also launching DoorDash Dot, a robot that delivers food to you rather than humans, which seems like a great idea. (Note the thick layer of sarcasm, reader.) The scary glimpse into our future continues as creators are rewarded. Short-form videos from local creators and foodies are now live in the DoorDash app; DoorDash hopes consumers will be able to preview dishes before ordering to more accurately see things like preparation style and portion size. This is starting in Atlanta, Austin, Miami, and San Francisco, with more rolling out through the end of the year.

Give the Gift of a DoorDash Gift Card

Not sure what to get your loved ones for their next birthday or holiday? A DoorDash gift card is the gift that never misses. Whether you want to ease the burden of planning dinners for new parents or you have a friend who’s always ordering takeout, a DoorDash gift card can be a thoughtful way to be there for your loved one when you can’t be there in person. There are many gift card styles, brands, and types, so you can rest assured there’s a gift for every occasion and every person.
